caption:
Guess 5 answers, then read. Before you read a chapter tonight, guess the answers to 5 of its end-of-chapter questions. Even wrong guesses help.

WHY: a question you've already tried to answer stays in your head while you read, so you notice its answer when it comes up. And a wrong guess that you then fix tends to stick better than an answer you simply read.

HOW:
1. Turn to the questions at the end of the chapter.
2. Write a quick guess for 5 of them. Wrong is fine.
3. Read the chapter.
4. When you reach each answer, check your guess and fix it.

THE RESEARCH: a preregistered 2024 review pooled the studies on guessing before you learn (St. Hilaire, Chan & Ahn, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review). Guessing first improved memory for the questioned material by a moderate amount (g = 0.54, 97 effects). In one of the first studies (Richland, Kornell & Kao 2009), people who tried questions before reading an essay did better on the later test, even on the questions they had got wrong at first.

THE CATCH: it helps with what the questions ask, not the rest of the chapter. The same review found almost no boost for material the questions didn't cover, so pick questions on what matters. You also have to read the real answers afterwards. 5 is our pick to keep it quick; the studies used different numbers of questions.

Do this tonight: Turn to the end. Guess 5 answers. Use the end-of-chapter questions. Then read, and check each one.

Send this to someone with a chapter to read tonight.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#studytips #studying #exam #focus #studyhacks
first_comment:
Sources (checked Nov 5 2026):
1) St. Hilaire, K. J., Chan, J. C. K. & Ahn, D. (2024). Guessing as a learning intervention: A meta-analytic review of the prequestion effect. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 31, 411-441 (online Aug 28 2023). doi:10.3758/s13423-023-02353-8. Preregistered meta-analysis: prequestions gave a moderate specific effect on the prequestioned information (g = 0.54, k = 97) and a virtually nonexistent general effect on other material (g = 0.04, k = 91). Checked on the authors' accepted manuscript (NSF PAR).
2) Richland, L. E., Kornell, N. & Kao, L. S. (2009). The pretesting effect: Do unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance learning? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 15(3), 243-257. doi:10.1037/a0016496. 5 experiments: people who answered questions before reading an essay on vision did better on the later test than people given extra study time, even counting only questions they had failed on the pretest. Checked on PubMed (PMID 19751074).
3) Pan, S. C. & Carpenter, S. K. (2023). Prequestioning and pretesting effects: A review of empirical research, theoretical perspectives, and implications for educational practice. Educational Psychology Review. doi:10.1007/s10648-023-09814-5. Over 60 peer-reviewed articles; benefits occur when learners can study the correct answers afterwards, mostly for fairly discrete facts; effects on untested material are inconsistent. Checked on SpringerLink.
Limits: most studies used students and facts from texts or videos; the number of questions (5) is our choice, not the studies'.

caption:
2 drinks before bed? Less dream sleep. Today's word: Skip.

One Word No. 9. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: a drink can make you drowsy, but it changes how the night goes. It pushes back and shortens REM, the sleep stage where most vivid dreams happen.

THE RESEARCH: a 2025 review pooled 27 lab studies of healthy adults (Gardiner et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews). On average, alcohol cut REM sleep by about 11 minutes, and bigger doses cut more. The authors put the point where REM loss showed up at about 2 standard drinks. Falling asleep faster took a high dose, about 5 drinks, and by then REM loss was bigger still. Their verdict: using alcohol as a sleep aid "is not an appropriate strategy".

HOW:
1. On nights when sleep matters (a test, an early start), skip the drink before bed.
2. Wind down another way: a book, a warm shower, the lights down.

THE CATCH: their standard drink was 10 g of alcohol, a bit less than a can of beer, so 2 of theirs is less than 2 cans. The paper says 3 drinks in one place; we use the authors' own summary (2). Most drinks were given within 3 hours of bed, so the review couldn't say how early is early enough. Total sleep time didn't change clearly on average, and these were small lab studies.

Do this: Skip it. Wind down without a drink.

Send this to whoever swears by a nightcap.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #sleepbetter #alcohol #focus #oneword

Source (checked Nov 5 2026):
Gardiner, C., Weakley, J., Burke, L. M., Roach, G. D., Sargent, C., Maniar, N., Huynh, M., Miller, D. J., Townshend, A. & Halson, S. L. (2025). The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 80, 102030. doi:10.1016/j.smrv.2024.102030. 27 studies (37 alcohol conditions). REM sleep fell by 11.3 min on average (95% CI -20.8 to -1.8), about 40 min more per extra 1 g/kg; REM onset was delayed 18 min. Abstract: REM disruption followed a low dose (<=0.50 g/kg, 'approximately two standard drinks'); sleep onset was only shortened at a high dose (>=0.85 g/kg, about five drinks). Total sleep time -10.1 min, not significant. Conclusion: alcohol as a sleep aid is not an appropriate strategy. Checked on the open-access PDF (ACU Research Bank).
Limits: lab studies of healthy adults; 21 of 27 studies had some risk of bias; a standard drink was 10 g of alcohol, and the paper's Results section gives the low-dose cut-off as up to 3 drinks.
